details.title: MA3491 - Fields and Applications
exam_block: The same topic blocks recur across all papers.
The official learning outcomes align almost exactly with the exam patterns.
Hamming codes, cyclic codes, finite field arithmetic, generator/check matrices and bounds are very consistent.
Recent papers from 2022-2023 onward have a nearly identical 5-question structure.
The module is algebra/coding-theory heavy; errors in finite-field arithmetic can cascade.
The format changed from 4 to 5 questions, though content stayed stable.
Current page staff do not exactly match all co-examiners, but Emil Skoldberg is the starred recent lecturer and is listed on the current page.
drill: The paper is highly repeatable: most years cover bounds, finite fields, linear codes, decoding, Hamming codes and cyclic codes.
Start with code bounds and block-code basics: sphere packing, Singleton, minimum distance, perfect/MDS codes and structured codeword counts.
Finite fields are central: irreducibility, factorisation, constructing fields such as F8 / F16 / F25 / F27 , field multiplication, inverses and primitive elements.
Linear-code calculations are high-return: generator matrices, standard form, parity-check matrices, minimum distance and codeword membership.
Decoding is very drillable: syndrome tables, standard arrays and nearest-neighbour decoding.
Hamming and cyclic codes are among the safest topics: parity-check construction, single-error correction, generator/check polynomials and cyclic-shift arguments.
Weight enumerators appeared in 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2025/26. In 2025/26 they were paired with a cyclic-code question and MacWilliams' identity, so they are now a recurring secondary topic.
details.name: Fields and Applications

families.title: Bounds And Parameters Of A Described Block Code
families.answer: Complete answer must contain: for a q -ary code C of length n and minimum distance d , set t = ⌊( d − 1)/2⌋ and state |C| Σ i=0 t C( n , i )( q − 1) i ≤ q n . Then substitute q , n , and t , divide by the sphere size, and take the integer upper bound. “Corrects all single errors” means t = 1, equivalently d ≥ 3.

families.title: Finite Fields And Polynomial Arithmetic
families.answer: Standard proof strategy: a degree-2 or degree-3 polynomial over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in that field, so test every field element. For a degree-5 polynomial over F 2 , rule out a linear factor and the irreducible quadratic x 2 + x + 1; otherwise any proper factorisation would have a factor of degree 1 or 2. For factorisation, first find roots, divide, and continue until every factor is irreducible.

families.title: Linear Codes, Minimum Distance, And Decoding
families.answer: Construction and checks: row-reduce G over the stated field to G = [ I k | A ]. Then a parity-check matrix is H = [− A T | I n−k ], with G H T = 0. A row vector v is a codeword exactly when vH T = 0. For a linear code, d min is the least nonzero codeword weight; enumerate the small code or use the smallest number of linearly dependent columns of H . To prove C = C ⊥ , show self-orthogonality (for example GG T = 0) and use dim C = dim C ⊥ = n /2.

families.title: Hamming Codes
families.answer: Complete answer must contain: Ham( r , q ) = { c ∈ F q n : cH T = 0}, where H is an r × n parity-check matrix whose columns are one representative from each one-dimensional subspace of F q r , and n = ( q r − 1)/( q − 1). Its parameters are [ n , n − r , 3]. For a single error ae j , the syndrome is ah j , so identify the column and scalar, subtract the error, and give the corrected word. For perfection, radius-1 balls are disjoint because d = 3 and have size 1 + n ( q − 1) = q r ; multiplying by |C| = q n − r gives q n , all ambient words.

families.title: Cyclic Codes, Weight Enumerators, And MacWilliams’ Identity
families.question: Distinct 2024/25 extension, Q5(b), 4 marks: for a binary cyclic code of odd length containing an odd-weight word u , prove it contains the all-ones word. Sum all cyclic shifts of u : each coordinate is the sum of wt( u ) ones, hence is 1 in F 2 .
families.answer: Complete construction: view a length- n cyclic code as an ideal in F q [ x ]/( x n − 1), generated by a monic divisor g ( x ) of x n − 1. If deg g = n − k , rows from the coefficient vectors of g , xg , …, x k −1 g give G . Compute h ( x ) = ( x n − 1)/ g ( x ). A standard check matrix is a generator matrix for C ⊥ : use the reciprocal h * ( x ) = h (0) −1 x deg h h ( x −1 ) as its generator polynomial; rows are its n − k shifts h * , xh * , …, x n − k −1 h * . Verify GH T = 0.

cards.back: For C ⊆ F q n with minimum distance d and t = ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋: |C| Σ i=0 t C(n,i)(q − 1) i ≤ q n . The sum is the radius-t Hamming-ball size; such balls about codewords are disjoint.

cards.front: 2. Apply sphere packing; define one-error correction.
cards.back: Calculate t, evaluate S = Σ C(n,i)(q−1) i , then |C| ≤ ⌊q n /S⌋. “Corrects every single error” means t ≥ 1, equivalently d ≥ 3. Show the substitution and integer bound.
|C| ≤ q n−d+1 . For a linear [n,k,d] code this is k ≤ n − d + 1.
Delete d−1 coordinates. Equal shortened images of distinct codewords would make them differ in at most d−1 places, impossible. Deletion is injective into F q n−d+1 , so |C| ≤ q n−d+1 .

cards.front: 5. Find parameters of a code defined by word conditions.
cards.back: Count permitted words for |C|. Prove a lower bound for distance and exhibit a pair attaining it. Only write [n,k,d] after establishing linearity and |C|=q k ; otherwise state length, size, distance.
|P 2k,q |=q k , d min =2; |P 2k+1,q |=q k+1 , d min =1. Binary length-8 weight-4 words: size C(8,4)=70, distance 2; changes must balance 0→1 and 1→0.

The q-ary length-n repetition code is [n,1,n], MDS because 1=n−n+1. It is perfect only if |C| times its radius-⌊(n−1)/2⌋ sphere size is q n . Ternary length 7: radius-3 sphere is 379 and 3·379 ≠ 3 7 , so not perfect.

cards.front: 8. Test degree-2/3 irreducibility over F q .
cards.back: A degree-2 or degree-3 polynomial over a field is irreducible iff it has no root in that field. Evaluate every a ∈ F q ; a root yields x−a. Divide and continue if factorisation is requested.

cards.front: 9. Prove a degree-5 polynomial over F 2 irreducible.
cards.back: Rule out roots 0 and 1, then rule out the only irreducible quadratic x 2 +x+1 by division. Any nontrivial degree-5 factorisation has a factor of degree 1 or 2, so this proves irreducibility.

cards.front: 10. Factor a polynomial over a finite field.
cards.back: Test all field elements for roots and divide out each linear factor. Factor the remainder by degree; a quadratic/cubic with no root is irreducible. Retain multiplicities and justify every final factor.
If p is irreducible of degree m, the quotient is a field of q m elements. Representatives have degree < m. Add in F q ; multiply and reduce using p(x)=0.

cards.front: 12. Multiply residue classes in a quotient field.
cards.back: Multiply representatives, then replace high powers using p(x)=0 until degree < deg p. Reduce coefficients in F q throughout and state the final reduced representative.
Use extended Euclid to find u,v with u(x)a(x)+v(x)p(x)=1. Modulo p, [u][a]=[1], so [u]=[a] −1 . Reduce u to degree < deg p and check the product if practical.
ord(a) is least positive m with a m =1. Since |F × |=|F|−1, a is primitive iff ord(a)=|F|−1. Test divisors of |F|−1 to find an order.

cards.front: 15. Prove a primitive inverse is primitive.
cards.back: (a −1 ) n =(a n ) −1 , so (a −1 ) n =1 iff a n =1. Thus a and a −1 have the same order. If a has order |F|−1, so does its inverse.
If F 4 =F 2 (a), {1,a} is an F 2 -basis. An F 4 -basis {e 1 ,…,e n } becomes F 2 -basis {e 1 ,…,e n ,ae 1 ,…,ae n }. Expand coefficients as u+va for spanning and independence.

cards.front: 17. Prove (a+b) p =a p +b p in characteristic p.
cards.back: Expand by the binomial theorem. For 0<j<p, the prime p divides C(p,j), so intermediate terms vanish in characteristic p. The endpoints remain.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: Use row operations over the stated field until G=[I k |A]. Row operations change the basis of the row space, not the code. Reduce arithmetic in F q .

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: From G=[I k |A], take H=[−A T |I n−k ]. Then GH T =0, and row vector v is in C iff vH T =0. H is (n−k)×n.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.front: 20. Find d min from codeword weights.
cards.back: List all nonzero linear combinations of generator rows, calculate their weights, and take the least. For a linear code, d min is the minimum nonzero codeword weight. Exhibit a word attaining it.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.front: 21. Find d min from H columns.
cards.back: d min is the smallest number of linearly dependent columns of H. No zero column gives d≥2; no proportional pair gives d≥3. Exhibit a dependent set for equality. Include all nonzero scalar multiples over F q .

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: Show C⊆C ⊥ , e.g. GG T =0. Then dim C ⊥ =n−dim C. If dim C=n/2, the included subspaces have equal dimension, so C=C ⊥ .

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: For received r, calculate s=rH T . Choose minimum-weight coset leader e with eH T =s; decode to r−e. In nonbinary codes, syndrome ah j identifies error ae j , including position and magnitude.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: In a standard array, locate r and decode to its top-row column word. Nearest-neighbour decoding gives codeword(s) at minimum Hamming distance. They agree when the chosen leader has minimum weight; state a tie if present.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: Let n=(q r −1)/(q−1), and H have one representative from each 1-dimensional subspace of F q r as columns. Ham(r,q)={c∈F q n :cH T =0}; its parameters are [n,n−r,3].

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: Choose one nonzero vector from every 1-dimensional subspace of F q r ; never include scalar multiples twice. There are (q r −1)/(q−1) columns. No two are proportional, supporting d min =3.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: If r=c+ae j , then rH T =ah j . Find the unique proportional column and scalar a, then correct to r−ae j . State corrected word, location, and magnitude if asked.

cards.group: Linear Codes, Decoding, And Hamming Codes
cards.back: d=3 makes radius-1 balls disjoint. Each has 1+n(q−1)=q r words; the code has q n−r words. The total q n−r q r =q n is the whole ambient space, so every word lies in exactly one ball.

cards.front: 29. Construct G from a cyclic generator polynomial.
cards.back: In F q [x]/(x n −1), let monic g divide x n −1. If deg g=n−k, coefficient vectors of g,xg,…,x k−1 g form the k×n generator matrix.
h(x)=(x n −1)/g(x). The dual generator is h * (x)=h(0) −1 x deg h h(x −1 ). Rows from h * ,xh * ,…,x n−k−1 h * form H; verify GH T =0.

cards.front: 31. Prove the odd-weight binary cyclic theorem.
cards.back: Sum all n cyclic shifts of an odd-weight codeword u. The sum remains in C. Every coordinate contains every entry of u once, so equals wt(u)=1 mod 2. Thus the all-ones word is in C.

cards.front: 32. Define and compute a weight enumerator.
cards.back: W C (z)=Σ c∈C z wt(c) . List all codewords, calculate weights, and collect equal exponents. Constant term is 1 and W C (1)=|C| checks the count.

cards.front: 33. State MacWilliams’ identity and find distance.
cards.back: For binary C length n: W C ⊥ (z)=|C| −1 (1+z) n W C ((1−z)/(1+z)). Apply it in the required direction. Minimum distance is the least positive exponent with nonzero coefficient.

cards.front: 34. Define Hamming distance and prove it is a metric.
cards.back: d(x,y) counts unequal coordinates. It is nonnegative, zero exactly when x=y, and symmetric. Coordinatewise 1 x≠z ≤1 x≠y +1 y≠z ; sum to obtain the triangle inequality.
ISBN-10: 10d 1 +9d 2 +…+d 10 ≡0 (mod 11), with X=10. ISBN-13: alternating weights 1,3,…,1 yield sum ≡0 (mod 10). Substitute an unknown and solve.
Exactly F × , the nonzero constants. If fg=1, deg f+deg g=0, so both have degree 0; every nonzero constant has scalar inverse. In a Euclidean domain, a unit u has uv=1 for some v.

sheets.title: Coding Bounds and Block-Code Parameters
sheets.purpose: Bounds say what size a q-ary code can possibly have, and let you recognise perfect and MDS cases. Exam use: q,n,M,d,t, ball volume, integer rounding and comparison/interpretation of bounds are shown.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: A binary (n=7,M=16,d=3) code has t=1. Sphere packing gives 16(1+7)=128=2 7 , so it is perfect. Singleton gives 16≤2 5 .

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: For a binary (n=7,d=3) code, t=1 and a Hamming ball has volume C(7,0)+C(7,1)=8. Therefore M*8<=2^7=128, so M<=16. The [7,4,3] Hamming code has M=2^4=16 and meets equality, hence is perfect. Singleton only gives M<=2^5=32 and is weaker here.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Apply Singleton to a ternary (5,M,3) code. Check: M≤3 3 =27.
practice.route: 2. Prove the Singleton bound, then decide whether a binary (5,4,3) code is perfect. Check: write the puncturing argument; t=1 gives 4(1+5)=24≠32, so not perfect.
practice.answer: 2. Prove the Singleton bound, then decide whether a binary (5,4,3) code is perfect. Check: write the puncturing argument; t=1 gives 4(1+5)=24≠32, so not perfect.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: bound a ternary length-6 code with d=3. Check t=1, ball volume 1+6(3-1)=13, so M<=floor(3^6/13)=56; Singleton gives M<=3^4=81, so Hamming is stronger.
practice.route: bound a ternary length-6 code with d=3. Check t=1, ball volume 1+6(3-1)=13, so M<=floor(3^6/13)=56; Singleton gives M<=3^4=81, so Hamming is stronger.
practice.answer: bound a ternary length-6 code with d=3. Check t=1, ball volume 1+6(3-1)=13, so M<=floor(3^6/13)=56; Singleton gives M<=3^4=81, so Hamming is stronger.

practice.title: Practice question - choose and apply a bound [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Bound the size M of a ternary length-6 code with minimum distance 3 using sphere packing and Singleton, and say which is stronger. [8 marks]
practice.route: t is floor((d-1)/2), not d-1.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: d=3 gives t=1; calculate the q-ary ball volume before comparing numerical bounds.

mistakes: Using d rather than t in the ball radius.
Calling equality in Singleton “perfect”; it means MDS.
Forgetting (q−1) i .
Recovery rule: Use t=floor((d-1)/2), not d-1; otherwise the Hamming balls correspond to a decoding radius the code cannot guarantee.

sheets.title: Cyclic Codes and Generator Polynomials
sheets.purpose: Cyclic codes convert shift closure into polynomial divisibility and give efficient encoders. Exam use: Field, modulus x^n-1, divisor test, dimension, coefficient order and final remainder/codeword are explicit.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: Over F 2 , x 3 −1=x 3 +1=(x+1)(x 2 +x+1). Choose g=x+1. Then k=2 and c=(1+x)(1+x)=1+x 2 , the word 101; h=x 2 +x+1.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Over F_2, n=7 and g(x)=x^3+x+1 gives k=4. For m(x)=x^3+x, c=m g=(x^3+x)(x^3+x+1)=x^6+x^3+x^2+x (middle x^4 terms cancel). Coefficient vector from x^0 to x^6 is (0,1,1,1,0,0,1). Multiplying by x modulo x^7-1 gives 1+x^2+x^3+x^4, another multiple modulo the quotient, so the shift stays in C.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. For the example, find k for g=x 2 +x+1. Check: k=1.
practice.route: 2. Factor x 7 −1 over F 2 , choose a divisor g, state [n,k], and construct two codewords. Check: show g divides the modulus and keep polynomial coefficients in F 2 .
practice.answer: 2. Factor x 7 −1 over F 2 , choose a divisor g, state [n,k], and construct two codewords. Check: show g divides the modulus and keep polynomial coefficients in F 2 .

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: decide whether r(x)=x^6+x^4+x^3+x is in this code. Check division by g over F_2: subtract x^3g=x^6+x^4+x^3, leaving remainder x. The remainder is nonzero, so r is not a codeword; the subtraction is coefficient-wise XOR.
practice.route: decide whether r(x)=x^6+x^4+x^3+x is in this code. Check division by g over F_2: subtract x^3g=x^6+x^4+x^3, leaving remainder x. The remainder is nonzero, so r is not a codeword; the subtraction is coefficient-wise XOR.
practice.answer: decide whether r(x)=x^6+x^4+x^3+x is in this code. Check division by g over F_2: subtract x^3g=x^6+x^4+x^3, leaving remainder x. The remainder is nonzero, so r is not a codeword; the subtraction is coefficient-wise XOR.

practice.title: Practice question - membership by polynomial division [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Over F 2 , let C have length 7 and generator g=x 3 +x+1. Decide whether r=x 6 +x 4 +x 3 +x lies in C. [8 marks]
practice.route: subtraction equals addition only because coefficients are in F 2 .
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: a cyclic-code word is a multiple of g modulo x 7 -1; degree 6 permits direct division using XOR subtraction.

mistakes: Using any polynomial rather than a divisor of x n −1.
Reversing deg g and k.
Forgetting reduction modulo x n −1 for shifts.
Recovery rule: Coefficient order is a convention, but changing it midway changes the reported word even if the polynomial calculation is right.

sheets.title: Syndromes, Cosets and Decoding
sheets.purpose: Decoding turns a received word into the nearest plausible codeword. Exam use: Matrix orientation, mod-field arithmetic, syndrome-to-leader map, correction and zero-syndrome verification are shown.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: For H=[1 1 1] over F 2 , r=111 has syndrome 1. Choose leader e=001, giving c=110, a codeword. This table has several weight-one leaders with the same syndrome, so this particular code does not uniquely correct every one-bit error.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Use H with columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111 and receive r=1011010. XOR columns 1,3,4,6 gives 001 xor 011 xor 100 xor 110=000, so r is already a codeword. If r'=1011011, its syndrome is column 7=111; under single-error decoding flip bit 7 to recover r. The conclusion depends on the at-most-one-error assumption.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. With the above H, find the syndrome of 101. Check: 0, so it is a codeword.
practice.route: 2. Build a syndrome table for a given H with distinct nonzero columns and decode a received word. Check: explain why column i is the syndrome of an error in position i.
practice.answer: 2. Build a syndrome table for a given H with distinct nonzero columns and decode a received word. Check: explain why column i is the syndrome of an error in position i.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: if syndrome equals column 3 but the channel may introduce two errors, explain the ambiguity. Check e3 and any two-error pattern whose two columns XOR to column 3 share the syndrome; nearest-neighbour correction is a decoding choice, not proof of the true error.
practice.route: if syndrome equals column 3 but the channel may introduce two errors, explain the ambiguity. Check e3 and any two-error pattern whose two columns XOR to column 3 share the syndrome; nearest-neighbour correction is a decoding choice, not proof of the true error.
practice.answer: if syndrome equals column 3 but the channel may introduce two errors, explain the ambiguity. Check e3 and any two-error pattern whose two columns XOR to column 3 share the syndrome; nearest-neighbour correction is a decoding choice, not proof of the true error.

practice.title: Practice question - syndrome and decoding assumption [8 marks]
practice.prompt: A binary H has columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111. If r=1011011, decode under an at-most-one-error channel model. [8 marks]
practice.route: syndrome labels a position only under the exact stated column order.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: XOR columns at the 1 positions, match the syndrome to a column, flip that coordinate, then state the modelling assumption.

mistakes: Subtracting the syndrome from r instead of an error vector.
Assuming any code can correct one error.
Not specifying a leader when syndromes collide.
Recovery rule: A nonzero syndrome identifies a coset, not automatically the physical error unless the leader assumption is justified.

sheets.title: Arithmetic in Finite Fields
sheets.purpose: Accurate field arithmetic underpins inverse, order and coding calculations. Exam use: Base field, defining relation, expansion, every reduction and multiplication-back check are visible.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: In F 4 with α 2 +α+1=0, α 2 =α+1. Then (α+1)α=α 2 +α=1, so (α+1) −1 =α.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: In F_2[x]/(x^3+x+1), let alpha be the class of x, so alpha^3=alpha+1. Compute (alpha^2+1)(alpha^2+alpha)=alpha^4+alpha^3+alpha^2+alpha. Since alpha^4=alpha(alpha+1)=alpha^2+alpha and alpha^3=alpha+1, the sum is (alpha^2+alpha)+(alpha+1)+alpha^2+alpha=alpha+1.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. In this F 4 , calculate (α+1) 2 . Check: α 2 +1=α.
practice.route: 2. In F 8 with α 3 =α+1, find an inverse of α 2 +1. Check: use the Euclidean algorithm or test the seven nonzero elements and show the reduction.
practice.answer: 2. In F 8 with α 3 =α+1, find an inverse of α 2 +1. Check: use the Euclidean algorithm or test the seven nonzero elements and show the reduction.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: find (alpha+1)^{-1}. Check (alpha+1)(alpha^2+alpha)=alpha^3+alpha=1 using alpha^3=alpha+1, so the inverse is alpha^2+alpha.
practice.route: find (alpha+1)^{-1}. Check (alpha+1)(alpha^2+alpha)=alpha^3+alpha=1 using alpha^3=alpha+1, so the inverse is alpha^2+alpha.
practice.answer: find (alpha+1)^{-1}. Check (alpha+1)(alpha^2+alpha)=alpha^3+alpha=1 using alpha^3=alpha+1, so the inverse is alpha^2+alpha.

practice.title: Practice question - inverse in a quotient field [8 marks]
practice.prompt: In F 2 [x]/(x 3 +x+1), with α 3 =α+1, find (α+1) -1 . [8 marks]
practice.route: α is a residue class, not a number to which ordinary integer division applies.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: exhibit a candidate product reduced by the defining relation, then multiply back to 1.

mistakes: Treating α as an integer.
Reducing with the wrong sign in odd characteristic.
Using Fermat’s exponent p−2 instead of q−2.
Recovery rule: Over F_2, subtraction equals addition; do not carry signs or integer coefficients into the reduced polynomial.

sheets.title: Constructing Finite Fields
sheets.purpose: Construction questions test irreducibility, quotient notation and a usable representation for later arithmetic. Exam use: Prime p, degree m, complete irreducibility test, p^m representatives and defining reduction relation are given.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: Over F 2 , f=x 3 +x+1 has no roots (f(0)=f(1)=1), hence is irreducible. F 8 =F 2 [x]/(f), with α 3 =α+1 and elements a+bα+cα 2 .

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Construct F_9 using f(x)=x^2+1 over F_3. This fails: f(1)=2 but f(0)=1 and f(2)=4+1=2, so actually it has no root and is irreducible. Let alpha^2=-1=2. The nine elements are a+b alpha with a,b in F_3. For example (1+alpha)^2=1+2alpha+alpha^2=2alpha mod 3.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Construct F 4 . Check: use x 2 +x+1; α 2 =α+1.
practice.route: 2. Justify that x 2 +2 over F 5 is reducible or irreducible, then construct the appropriate quotient if irreducible. Check: test roots; 2 is not a square mod 5, so irreducible.
practice.answer: 2. Justify that x 2 +2 over F 5 is reducible or irreducible, then construct the appropriate quotient if irreducible. Check: test roots; 2 is not a square mod 5, so irreducible.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: Paper-style synthesis: explain why x^2+x+1 does not construct F_4 over F_2. Check f(1)=1+1+1=1 mod 2 and f(0)=1, so it actually has no root and is irreducible; therefore it does construct F_4. Correct the premise rather than forcing the requested conclusion.
practice.route: explain why x^2+x+1 does not construct F_4 over F_2. Check f(1)=1+1+1=1 mod 2 and f(0)=1, so it actually has no root and is irreducible; therefore it does construct F_4. Correct the premise rather than forcing the requested conclusion.
practice.answer: explain why x^2+x+1 does not construct F_4 over F_2. Check f(1)=1+1+1=1 mod 2 and f(0)=1, so it actually has no root and is irreducible; therefore it does construct F_4. Correct the premise rather than forcing the requested conclusion.

practice.title: Practice question - construct F 25 [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Show x 2 +x+1 is irreducible over F 5 , then present F 25 . [8 marks]
practice.route: testing only 0 and 1 is sufficient over F 2 , not over F 5 .
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: a quadratic is irreducible iff it has no root; evaluate all five residues, then give quotient, basis and reduction relation.

mistakes: Using a reducible modulus.
Writing x=α without stating the quotient.
Listing p m coefficients rather than p m elements.
Recovery rule: Evaluate roots in the base field with modular arithmetic; a question's suggested conclusion may be false and must not override the calculation.

sheets.title: Hamming Codes over Finite Fields
sheets.purpose: Hamming codes are a compact construction of perfect single-error-correcting q-ary codes. Exam use: Definition, parameters, column convention, syndrome arithmetic, correction, parity recheck and perfect-code count appear.

practice.title: Worked example
practice.prompt: For m=3, n=7. Take H with columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111. A syndrome 101 points to position 5, so flip bit 5.

practice.title: Medium/hard paper-style synthesis
practice.prompt: For m=3 choose H columns 001,010,011,100,101,110,111. If r=1101000, syndrome is 001 xor 010 xor 100=111, so flip bit 7 to get c=1101001. Recheck: 001 xor 010 xor 100 xor 111=000. The [7,4,3] code has 16 codewords and ball size 8, giving 16*8=128=2^7, hence perfect.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Give [n,k,d] for m=4. Check: [15,11,3].
practice.route: 2. Construct H for m=3, prove it corrects one error, and verify the sphere-packing equality. Check: include both distinct-column and counting arguments.
practice.answer: 2. Construct H for m=3, prove it corrects one error, and verify the sphere-packing equality. Check: include both distinct-column and counting arguments.

practice.title: Hard paper-style synthesis

practice.title: Practice question - Hamming correction and perfection [8 marks]
practice.prompt: For Ham(3,2) with all nonzero 3-bit H columns, explain one-error correction and verify perfection. [8 marks]
practice.route: a zero syndrome means no error only under the at-most-one-error model.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use distinct nonzero syndromes for correction and the sphere count for perfection.

mistakes: Including the zero column.
Using n=2 m rather than 2 m −1.
Reading syndrome bits in a different order from H.
Recovery rule: The binary value of a syndrome names a bit only if the column ordering uses that convention; otherwise locate the matching column directly.

sheets.purpose: Linear-code questions link matrix algebra over F q to size, membership and error detection. Exam use: Field, dimensions, convention, generated words, parity orthogonality and distance/error capability are consistent.

practice.title: Practice question - derive H and minimum distance [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Over F 2 , G=[[1,0,1,1],[0,1,1,0]]. Find H and d min . [8 marks]
practice.route: in nonbinary fields the left block is -P T , not P T without checking signs.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: recognise G=[I 2 |P], use H=[P T |I 2 ], then enumerate four codewords.

mistakes: Doing ordinary real-number arithmetic.
Counting rows of a non-full-rank G as k.
Calling the least row weight d without checking combinations.
Recovery rule: Minimum distance includes pairs of distinct codewords; only linearity permits replacing that search by minimum nonzero weight.

practice.title: Practice question - enumerator and duality [8 marks]
practice.prompt: For C={0000,1100,0110,1010}, find W C (z) and decide whether C is self-dual over F 2 . [8 marks]
practice.route: never infer self-dual solely from n=2k.
practice.answer: Demand diagnosis and fastest route: enumerate all supplied words, then compare C with C ⊥ , not just dimensions.

mistakes: Confusing perfect with MDS.
Counting only generator rows in a weight enumerator.
Claiming a BCH construction without specifying roots or a splitting field.
Recovery rule: Orthogonal complement depends on the field's dot product; integer arithmetic can give the wrong nullspace.
